background_notes.fact: For real alpha, f(s)=exp(-i*alpha*s) is smooth as a complex-valued function of real s, f'(s)=-i*alpha*f(s), |f(s)|=1, and |f(s)-f(r)|<=|alpha|*|s-r| for all real r,s. Consequently the h defined in S001 is smooth and |h'(s)|=|alpha|.

grounds.reason: The phases are fixed real numbers and h is this exponential minus its step average, which is constant in s.
For tau>0 the average is a scalar; the smooth exponential is integrable on [0,tau].

background_notes.justification: Differentiation of the complex exponential and the chain rule give f'. For real t, exp(i*t) has modulus one, so |f'|=|alpha|. The fundamental theorem of calculus applied to the real and imaginary parts, followed by the integral triangle inequality on the interval between r and s, gives the difference estimate. Subtracting a constant leaves the derivative unchanged. These are routine one-variable calculus facts for the explicit smooth function used by the supplied proof.

background_notes.fact: For tau>0 and a continuously differentiable complex h on [0,tau], normalized integration is linear, preserves constants, and satisfies |tau^(-1)*integral g|<=tau^(-1)*integral |g| for continuous complex g. For real beta!=0, tau^(-1)*integral_0^tau h(s)*exp(-i*beta*s) ds equals [h(s)*exp(-i*beta*s)]_0^tau/(-i*beta*tau) - (1/(-i*beta*tau))*integral_0^tau h'(s)*exp(-i*beta*s) ds, and its modulus is at most (|h(0)|+|h(tau)|+integral_0^tau |h'(s)| ds)/(tau*|beta|).

grounds.reason: tau>0 is assumed; h is a smooth exponential minus a constant, and the integration-by-parts step occurs in the branch where both phases are nonzero.
The averaging operator is exactly tau^(-1) times integration on [0,tau].
Linearity identifies the covariance with the integral of h(s)*exp(-i*beta*s).

background_notes.justification: On the compact interval all displayed functions and derivatives are continuous and integrable. Linearity and the integral norm bound apply componentwise to complex-valued integration. Integrating the derivative of h(s)*exp(-i*beta*s)/(-i*beta) proves the identity by the fundamental theorem of calculus. The triangle inequality and |exp(-i*beta*s)|=1 give the bound. These standard integration facts justify precisely the integration step already present in S001; there is no limiting interchange.
